event.family_marine_10_report_against_hi: Say you believe him
You take his side before knowing the details of the accusation.
Read the report anyway
You catch one sentence out of context and immediately read it against him.
The jargon leaves you with more suspicion than answers.
You understand the delay let civilians leave the area before the intervention.
You notice the report omits the civilians from its main summary.
Ask what he did
You refuse to choose between trust and accusation without hearing him speak.
The Report Against Him
An official summons reaches the household: your father is accused of delaying an order during an operation, allowing a target to escape. He asks you not to read the report.
Believe his reason
You separate the act he is accused of from the reason he gives.
Ask who can confirm it
You ask him for a witness, not a better story.
Say he still disobeyed
You refuse to let good intentions erase the chain of command.
What They Blame Him For
The report is true about one thing: your father did delay the order. He says he waited for three families to clear the quay before letting the patrol move in.
Support his choice, not his method
You refuse to turn the case into total innocence or guilt.
Defend his refusal fully
For you, the result justifies the risk he took against the order.
Say he should have reported it
You recognize the civilians were protected but reject him deciding the rule alone.
Another Version
A Marine collecting the summons confirms the civilians, but adds that your father could have warned his superior instead of acting alone.
Say you support him without absolving him
You keep the family bond without automatically declaring him right.
Say you stand with him
You choose loyalty to him when the institution is testing it.
Say you need to think
You refuse to produce a family answer just because a hearing demands one.
What You Owe Him
Before leaving for the hearing, your father asks only one thing: do not let his uniform decide for you what you think of him.
event.family_marine_10_they_discuss_your: Ask what they have planned
You enter the conversation instead of letting it define you from outside.
Interrupt them
Your interruption is treated as childish impatience and the conversation resumes over your head.
They listen for a second, then turn back to your father.
Both officers stop speaking about you in the third person.
One closes the file and asks you directly what you want to know.
Ask what happens if you say no
The room goes quiet before an adult finds an answer.
They Already Discuss Your Uniform
Two officers discuss a future recruitment file, your aptitude, and where “a child from this family” might begin. Nobody has asked whether you want to serve.
Ask for the conditions
You want to know what the favor expects in return.
Accept being watched
You accept the attention without yet promising the uniform.
Reject the plan
You refuse to let the file advance before your decision.
The Offer Before the Age
They speak of observation, recommendations, and an easier entry once Active begins. It is a promise, but also an expectation.
Let him sign
You let him commit the family to this preparation.
Take the pen from him
You remind everyone the file carries your name, not his.
Ask what he really wants
You force your father to separate his pride from your future.
What Your Father Does With It
Your father receives the pen meant for family authorization. The officers wait for him to speak before you.
Say you want to see where it leads
You accept the inheritance as a serious possibility, not yet an obligation.
Say it will be on your terms
You reject a prewritten future while keeping the Marine among your choices.
Say nobody will choose for you
You close the file without necessarily closing the door on the Marine itself.
Your Future Is Not Signed
The file remains open on the table. What matters now is not the paper, but how you accept or reject the expectation placed on you.
event.family_marine_10_argument_through_: Listen to the end
You stay close enough to hear what they avoided saying in front of you.
Enter the room
You refuse to let the argument continue as if it did not concern you.
Leave the house
You refuse to become the third argument in their fight.
The Argument Through the Wall
Your parents argue behind a partition. Your mother discovered your father accepted a more dangerous assignment without telling her. The word “family” comes up more often than “Marine.”
Say your mother is right about the decision
You separate the job from how your father treated the household.
Say the posting may matter
You acknowledge his work may have reasons beyond the household.
Say they should have decided together
You refuse to turn duty and family into permanent sides.
What the Posting Costs
The posting means less time at home, more danger, and a possible move. Your mother mainly blames your father for deciding alone.
Say you want him to stay
You answer the question even if it perhaps should never have been put to you.
Say you want to understand his mission
You refuse to ask only for comfort without understanding the work at stake.
Refuse to choose between them
You hand back the decision they had just placed on you.
“And You?”
The argument stops when one parent asks what you want. The other immediately says it is not your job to settle their problem.
Stay with your mother
Your mother becomes a real counterweight to the idea that service always decides first.
Stay with your father
You accept more of service's cost without erasing what it does to the household.
Ask them to decide together
You refuse to let their conflict become your permanent side.
After the Argument
The posting is not yet settled, but the question of how the family should decide together is clearer.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet.c: You first agree to protect what he told you.
You refuse to call it a secret without knowing who it protects.
You tell him his trust cannot decide what is true for everyone else.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet.t: After the stall incident, your father learns an internal report minimizes the vendor's losses. He asks you not to repeat what he admitted to you that evening.
event.family_marine_10_keep_this_quiet_i: Protect your father
You accept that truth can also hurt someone you love.
Think first of the vendor
You refuse to forget the person already paying the price of silence.
Look for a truth that does not accuse everyone
You look for what can be said without inventing or revealing everything.
Why Stay Quiet
Your father explains an inquiry could punish him and fall on the whole patrol. He does not say the report is fair; he says speaking will have a price.
Tell everything
You mix what you saw with what your father told you, weakening your account.
The investigator writes it down but repeatedly asks whether you are sure.
You clearly separate what you saw from what your father told you.
Your account forces the investigator to reopen the report section minimizing the losses.
Say only what you saw
You protect the confidence without lying about the lost crates.
Refuse to answer
You keep the secret at the cost of a question now visible in the file.
The Chance to Speak
The next day, an investigator simply asks whether you saw the losses at the stall. Your father is not in the room.
Say you kept his confidence
You protect your father, but you know exactly what that protection leaves out of the report.
Say you did not lie
You refuse to choose between betraying a confidence and denying what you saw.
Say truth came before him
You accept that your relationship pays part of the price for what you said.
What Silence Protects
When you return, your father asks what you said. For the first time, the secret is also a decision between you.
event.family_marine_10_tell_us_what_mari: Read the official text
You take the sheet and follow the prepared words exactly.
Speak in your own words
You stumble under the attention and one awkward phrase becomes what everyone remembers.
Your message comes out less clearly than in your head, but it is yours.
You tell a concrete experience instead of reciting a slogan.
The room stops looking at the official sheet and actually listens to you.
Give the microphone back
You refuse to be used as a ready-made answer to a question about your own life.
Tell Us What Marine Means
At a family ceremony, the organizer hands you the small microphone: “Tell us what it means to grow up in a Marine family.” The official text lies in front of you.
Repeat your point more clearly
You refuse to let a confused reaction replace what you meant.
Let the host conclude
You let the host return the ceremony to its planned frame.
Speak to the other children
You shift the conversation toward those who actually live what is being discussed.
The Room Reacts
Families, officers, and other children do not react the same way. The organizer tries to regain control of the moment.
Say the Marine must change
You state that the institution itself is part of the question.
Say your family is the subject
You refuse to turn every family difficulty into a political manifesto.
Say you were speaking about yourself
You refuse to stretch your words beyond what you lived.
What an Adult Hears
After the ceremony, a Marine stops you. He wants to know whether your words criticized the Marine itself or only how some families are treated.
Keep the ideal of protection
You separate what the Marine claims to protect from all the imperfect ways it does so.
Keep your own words
You decide nobody will define your inheritance for you.
Keep distance from the symbol
You accept your family without having to love how the institution stages it.
Your Own Definition
The microphone is put away, but the sentence you keep for yourself matters more than the one that will remain in the report.
You place your fingers on the letters as if checking they are real.
You refuse to let the plaque be the only available version.
You refuse to give the plaque the power to impose a memory on you.
Your father's name appears on a base plaque. Beneath it, one clean sentence summarizes his whole career. The old sergeant stops beside you without comment.
event.family_marine_10_his_name_on_wall_: Accept that plaques simplify
You accept that a wall is not a complete story.
Tell the sergeant what you remember
You rebuild aloud the less polished version you chose to keep.
Ask whether the wording can change
You ask whether official memory can still be corrected.
The Chosen Words
The plaque speaks of duty and courage. It says nothing about the broken bridge, the mistake, or what he had to repair.
Keep both versions
You let the plaque exist without giving it the final word.
Prefer the private memory
You choose the imperfect story nobody engraved.
Prefer the plaque
You choose the version that gives his service a clear, shareable shape.
Memory Does Not Belong to the Wall
The old sergeant tells you the plaque belongs to the base. What you say about your father belongs only to those who knew him.
Keep his complexity
You refuse to believe loving his memory requires simplifying it.
Keep his service
You choose to make his service a central part of what he left you.
Keep your name separate from his
You refuse to let his inscription automatically become your inheritance.
What Remains Yours
When you leave the wall, the name stays behind. The way you carry it leaves with you.
event.family_marine_10_giant_offer_too_e: Agree to hear it
You accept the meeting without accepting the program yet.
Ask for the terms first
The officer treats your request as needless suspicion and presents the program without answering precisely.
You get vague promises, not written limits.
The officer has to specify who can summon you, how often, and for what.
He agrees to write down your conditions before presenting his own.
Refuse the file
You refuse to let a program already exist around you without your agreement.
An Offer Too Early
An officer arrives with a file prepared for you: regular training, quarterly measurements, and access to Marine equipment. You are only ten, but the program already talks about your future.
Focus on training
You separate what can genuinely teach you something from the rest of the program.
Point at the demonstrations
You ask why your learning must be shown to people who do not train you.
Point at the tracking
You ask when the program stops measuring and starts actually teaching you.
The Program
The file provides for tests, growth tracking, and occasional demonstrations before senior staff. It promises adapted equipment and privileged access to instructors.
Say strength is for protection
You bring the program back to what you did during the previous demonstration.
Say you are not a weapon
You reject language that talks about your body before it talks about you.
Accept being evaluated
You accept that your potential interests the Marine as long as participation remains your choice.
What They Want From You
The officer finally uses the words “strategic potential.” He says the Marine wants to know what a Giant trained early might contribute later.
Make them write your limits
The officer rewrites your limits as optional recommendations.
He accepts some limits but refuses to make them binding.
He writes that demonstrations require your agreement and that training takes priority over spectacle.
He signs the limits himself and has the document countersigned before returning it to you.
Refuse unless it is written
You refuse to let verbal promises commit years of your life.
Accept without adding clauses
You accept the program as offered.
Your Conditions
You now have the file, the pen, and the officer's attention. If the program continues, this is where your limits can become written.
Keep a signed copy
Your limits now exist in the same administrative language as their expectations.
Refuse further tracking
You leave the program rather than accept limits the Marine can ignore.
Accept the program as written
You choose access and training despite what the file expects from your body.
What Stays in the File
The file finally closes. What it contains will determine whether the next offer treats you as a person to train or a resource to exploit.
You let the presentation unfold as the officers prepared it.
Your interruption is drowned by applause and the official immediately takes the microphone back.
You speak, but the official immediately summarizes your words his way.
The visitors stop looking at the official and look at you.
You completely reverse the presentation: questions now come directly to you.
Leave the center of the yard
You refuse to be living proof of a sentence nobody asked you to approve.
During an official visit, a senior Marine places you at the center of a yard and presents you as “proof the Marine knows how to make room for everyone.” You recognize the staging before he finishes.
event.family_marine_10_giant_on_display_: Show only what you chose
You limit the demonstration to what you had previously agreed to.
Explain how you got your limits
You make visible that this place was never offered without conflict.
Say you represent only yourself
You refuse to be used as general proof about all Giants or all families.
What the Crowd Sees
The visitors watch you as much as the uniform around you. The scene can still serve the official staging, or become something else.
Let him conclude
You get peace at the price of letting him narrate your opposition his way.
Correct him in front of the visitors
You refuse to let your consent be invented after the fact.
Ask the crowd what they heard
You take away the official's monopoly on the conclusion.
Saving the Presentation
The official tries to conclude that your freedom to speak proves the system works. He turns your refusal into an argument for himself.
Keep the last word
You turn the display into a statement nobody had planned.
Accept being a symbol
You accept your image serving an institution you still believe can keep its promise.
Decide this was the last time
You close the door on any further staging of your body.
Your Voice or Their Symbol
As the yard empties, you know whether the visitors will leave with your story or only the image the Marine wanted to display.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey.c: You follow the order, hoping someone will reach the injured civilian another way.
The gate nearly tears your hands away and jams halfway in a dangerous position.
You cannot hold it alone and a Marine forces you to let go.
You gain enough time for the injured civilian to reach the opening.
You hold the gate until a Marine finally helps you instead of closing it.
You refuse to choose immediately between the gate and the person.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey.t: A fire breaks out near a dock warehouse. The order is to close the gate to contain the crowd, but an injured civilian is still on the other side as the lock begins to drop.
event.family_marine_10_protect_or_obey_i: Hold the line
You help prevent the crowd from turning the fire into a larger disaster.
Go through to help the injured person
You make the trapped person your immediate priority.
Use a rope over the barrier
You look for a solution that does not reopen the gate to the whole crowd.
The Gate Comes Down
The smoke thickens. The watch commander repeats the order because the crowd is already pressing from the other side of the dock.
Disobey and continue
You get trapped too and two Marines have to come get both of you.
You help poorly and complicate the maneuver before the Marines regain control.
You reach the injured civilian and bring them to the safe passage.
You protect the injured civilian while guiding others toward an exit that does not reopen the crowd.
Return behind the gate
You obey the final order and leave the rescue to the adults.
Force a third solution
Your idea comes too late and briefly distracts the adults from the useful maneuver.
The idea does not work fast enough; the commander refuses to change the plan.
You find a route that preserves the closure while reaching the injured civilian.
Your solution becomes the post's new plan for the rest of the fire.
The Choice Becomes Real
The injured civilian slips to the ground. The watch commander sees you act and gives one final clear order: “Get back behind the gate.”
Say the order was protecting people too
You refuse to caricature the order simply because it had a visible cost.
Say an order is not enough
You state that a rule must still be judged by what it actually protects.
Say another solution was needed
You reject the idea that the only options were obedience or opening everything.
After the Order
The fire is contained. The watch commander calls you aside: he wants to know whether you understand your action may have saved someone and endangered others.
Keep discipline as a safeguard
You accept that protection without a framework can become another danger.
Keep protection before obedience
You decide an order loses legitimacy when it demands abandoning someone who can still be saved.
Keep the third way
You refuse to let authority make you forget that a situation can be changed rather than merely endured.
What You Call Duty
When you return home, you no longer have only an opinion about one order: you have a personal definition of what duty must protect.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty.cho: You protect the house at the expense of the rest.
You prioritize evenings when someone still needs to work or read.
You prioritize what lets your father continue serving.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty.tex: A pay deduction arrives after one of your father's missions. This month the household must choose between repairing a leak, buying more lamp oil, or replacing worn boots.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty_i01: You accept that holding a household together sometimes means choosing which problem waits.
Ask your father what he would sacrifice
You refuse to let his work create a shortage he alone does not have to face.
You look for how to reduce several problems instead of solving one perfectly.
The first purchase solves one problem and makes the other two more visible. The household can no longer pretend service's cost exists only on paper.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_duty_i02: You refuse to let every family shortage be automatically absorbed in the name of service.
Accept that service has a price
You accept more fully that the household also pays for what it believes matters.
Ask him to make it up another way
You reject the choice between total support and rejection: duty must also give something back to the household.
Your father looks over the accounts with you. For once, duty's cost is neither a grand idea nor a mission: it is what is missing from the table.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_family.c: You step forward when the clerk opens the way.
You stay in the line where you arrived.
Ask whether your neighbor can pass too
You turn the personal privilege into a question for the clerk.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_family.t: In a base queue, a clerk recognizes your family name and offers to move you ahead “for services rendered.” The other families hear perfectly.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_family_i: You refuse to pretend the advantage does not exist.
Say you did not earn it
You clearly separate family history from your personal merit.
Use the access to help someone
You look for a way to turn the advantage into something that does not stop with you.
Whether you move ahead or not, everyone now knows your name can open a door faster than theirs.
You accept the inheritance but attach an obligation toward others to it.
You refuse to let your father's service become your automatic shortcut.
Use the system without idealizing it
You learn that knowing rules and access does not require confusing them with justice.
What You Do With the Name
The line finally moves. The privilege is no longer hypothetical: you decided what to do when the family name acts before you.
event.family_marine_10_fallback_identity: Carry the sign
You accept the role prepared for you.
Ask to change how it is done
You accept the ceremony, not necessarily the exact place assigned to you.
Refuse to represent the group
You refuse to let one person serve as a summary of every family present.
What They Expect From You
For a local ceremony, the family office asks you to carry the small sign leading the Marine relatives' procession. “You'll represent the group well,” the clerk says.
Explain why you accepted
You give the role your own meaning before the clerk does it for you.
Offer to share the role
You refuse to let representation rest on one person.
Return the sign before departure
You change your mind before the procession turns your presence into a symbol.
The Group Gets Ready
The other families arrive and immediately see the place you were given. Some think it natural; others ask why you.
Say you represent your family
You accept the family inheritance without pretending to speak for the whole Marine.
Say you represent only yourself
You refuse to let family affiliation turn your identity into a public function.
Accept carrying the symbol
You accept the Marine as part of what you want to show the world.
What You Agree to Represent
The procession begins with or without you at the front. What remains is the boundary you draw between belonging to a Marine family and representing the whole institution.
